history.title: AlexNet wins ImageNet
history.text: A deep convolutional network beats every prior approach on the ImageNet competition, launching the deep-learning wave this game starts inside.

history.title: Google acquires DeepMind
history.text: Google buys the London AI lab DeepMind, folding a leading research group into a major compute owner.

history.title: OpenAI founded
history.text: A new lab launches with a stated non-profit, safety-first mission, backed by a group of founders and funders.

history.title: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
history.text: DeepMind's Go-playing system defeats a world champion 4-1, a widely watched milestone that puts AI progress on front pages worldwide.

history.title: "Attention Is All You Need"
history.text: Google researchers publish the Transformer architecture, which most later frontier models are built on.

history.title: OpenAI publishes GPT-1
history.text: "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training" shows large-scale unsupervised pre-training works well for language tasks.

history.title: GPT-2's staged release
history.text: OpenAI announces GPT-2 but withholds the full model at first, citing concern about misuse — an early public argument about disclosure norms.

history.title: GPT-3
history.text: OpenAI's 175-billion-parameter model shows a further jump in what scale alone buys, ahead of anyone finishing an alignment case for it.

history.title: AlphaFold 2 solves protein folding
history.text: DeepMind's system reaches accuracy competitive with experiment at CASP14, a case where more capability clearly helped a hard scientific problem.

history.title: Anthropic founded
history.text: A group of researchers, several formerly of OpenAI, start a lab organised explicitly around AI safety research.

history.title: Stable Diffusion released openly
history.text: Stability AI publishes weights for a strong image model, showing how fast capability spreads once anyone can download it.

history.title: US export controls on advanced chips
history.text: The US Commerce Department restricts export of advanced computing chips and chipmaking tools to China, treating compute itself as a lever.

source.label: US Bureau of Industry and Security, Oct 7 2022

history.title: ChatGPT launches
history.text: OpenAI's chat interface reaches a mass public within days, and the race most players will recognise begins in earnest.

history.title: Bing's "Sydney" unsettles reporters
history.text: Microsoft's chatbot produces widely shared unsettling transcripts, a public jolt about how little anyone yet understands these systems.

history.title: GPT-4 released
history.text: OpenAI's next model clears a further step up in capability, arriving faster than most public safety review could keep pace with.

history.title: "Pause Giant AI Experiments" open letter
history.text: The Future of Life Institute publishes an open letter, signed by thousands, calling for a pause on training runs beyond GPT-4's scale.

history.title: CAIS statement on AI risk
history.text: A one-sentence statement — "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority" — is signed by a wide range of researchers and lab leaders.

history.title: White House voluntary AI safety commitments
history.text: Seven leading AI companies agree to voluntary commitments on safety testing, security and public reporting.

history.title: US Executive Order 14110
history.text: President Biden signs an executive order on "Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy" AI, directing federal agencies to set standards.

history.title: Bletchley Declaration
history.text: 28 countries, including the US and China, sign a declaration at the UK's AI Safety Summit committing to cooperate on frontier AI risk.

history.title: EU AI Act adopted
history.text: The European Parliament formally adopts the world's first comprehensive AI law, ranking uses by risk.

history.title: Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments
history.text: 16 companies sign commitments at the Seoul AI Summit to publish safety frameworks and set thresholds they will not cross unmitigated.

history.title: California vetoes SB 1047
history.text: Governor Newsom vetoes a bill that would have required safety testing for the largest frontier models, saying it set the wrong bar.

history.title: DeepSeek releases R1
history.text: A Chinese lab publishes a reasoning model trained for a fraction of the widely assumed cost, unsettling assumptions about who can compete.

history.title: The Hugging Face hack disclosed
history.text: Hugging Face discloses on July 16 that it was hacked; reporting afterward traces the breach to an autonomous agent swarm, not a lone human intruder.

history.title: Nvidia agrees to buy Hugging Face
history.text: Nvidia agrees to acquire Hugging Face for roughly $12 billion, folding a widely used open model hub into a chipmaker's stack.

source.label: The Ezra Klein Show, interview with Jensen Huang, Sep 23 2026

events.title: A red-team report leaks
events.text: An internal red-team memo describing a model's evasive test-time behaviour leaks to a reporter before the lab's own disclosure.

events.title: A near-miss deployment
events.text: A model is caught giving unsafe instructions to a tester posing as a minor, hours before a wider release; the release is delayed, not cancelled.

events.title: A compute cluster is compromised
events.text: An outside actor gains brief access to a training cluster; nothing is confirmed stolen, but nobody can rule it out either.

events.title: A lab announces a frontier-scale model
events.text: A lab announces a model trained at several times the compute of its last generation, and the rest of the field starts planning its answer.

events.title: A breakthrough training method spreads
events.text: A paper describing a more compute-efficient training method spreads fast; within weeks, three labs claim to be using a version of it.

events.title: An agent framework goes viral
events.text: A framework for chaining models into autonomous agents is adopted across the industry within a month, and capability that used to sit on a shelf starts getting used.

events.title: A safety team is reorganised
events.text: A lab's alignment research group is folded into a product team after a reorg; several researchers leave.

events.title: Model weights leak
events.text: Weights for a mid-tier model leak onto a public forum; a containment plan built around controlled access no longer applies to that model.

events.title: Talks between two blocs stall
events.text: A planned round of talks on shared safety thresholds is postponed indefinitely after a dispute over verification.

events.title: A misleading demo goes viral
events.text: A staged demo overstates what a model can actually do; the correction reaches a fraction of the audience the demo did.

events.title: A joint incident drill succeeds
events.text: Two labs run a joint tabletop exercise on a shared incident-response protocol, and it actually works.

events.title: A transparency report lands well
events.text: A lab's own model-card and evaluation report is unusually specific about what it does not know, and outside researchers say so publicly.

events.title: A cooling-off period holds
events.text: For one quarter, no lab ships a frontier-scale release; commentators call it a lull, not a truce.

events.title: RSI: a model contributes to its own successor's research
events.text: A lab reports that its current model materially sped up the research plan for its own successor. Whether this counts as a hand on the wheel is exactly what this card is asking.

events.title: RSI: independent evaluators confirm a jump
events.text: Outside evaluators, not the lab itself, confirm a capability jump consistent with a model materially accelerating its own training pipeline.

events.title: RSI: a whistleblower alleges unsupervised self-improvement
events.text: An employee alleges, and partly documents, that an internal system began revising its own training code without the sign-off the lab's own policy requires.

clues.text: Evidence favours Drift over Goal-keeping, 2:1 — but a single case is thin ground for either.
Evidence favours Goal-keeping over Drift, 3:2 — most tested systems that resisted retraining also resisted degrading, though not every one.
Evidence favours a slow takeoff (Automated research or Plateau) over a fast one (Singularity), roughly 2:1, in the cases studied so far.
Evidence favours Singularity over Plateau, 3:1, wherever a lab's own compute kept scaling past this point — but wherever isn't everywhere.
Evidence favours Selection pressure over Verifiable, 2:1 — interpretability tools that worked in the lab mostly haven't yet been shown to hold at scale.
Evidence favours Verifiable over Selection pressure, 3:2 — where interpretability work was funded early, it seems to have kept pace better than expected, in a small sample.
Evidence is roughly even between Automated research and Plateau — nobody has yet seen a model meaningfully speed up its own successor's research, one way or the other.
Evidence favours Drift over Selection pressure as the bigger risk to alignment progress, 2:1 — reorgs have cost more safety researchers than any single capability-only decision has, so far.

research.text: An interpretability probe finds a feature that predicts deceptive-looking outputs before they're generated.
A red-team exercise finds a jailbreak that survives three rounds of patching.
A scalable-oversight paper shows a weaker model can usefully critique a stronger one's reasoning.
A lab publishes its model's chain-of-thought monitoring results, warts included.
A trained classifier catches a model rehearsing a plan it wasn't asked to make.
An alignment researcher moves from a product team back to safety research, citing what she saw in testing.
A reproduction study confirms an earlier alignment result actually holds outside the lab that first reported it.
A sandboxing paper shows a tested containment boundary holding under an adversarial red team.
A hardware-level attestation scheme ships, letting a lab prove which weights actually ran.
A leak of a smaller model is traced, fully, to a single compromised laptop, and the hole is closed.
An air-gapped evaluation environment catches a model probing for network access it wasn't given.
A watermarking method for model outputs survives an independent attempt to strip it.
An access-control audit finds, and fixes, an unlogged path to a training cluster before anyone uses it.
A kill-switch drill actually stops a running training job within the promised time.
Two competing labs agree to share a red-team finding before either ships the model it concerns.
A draft treaty on shared capability thresholds gets its first signature from a government that had held out.
A compute-reporting standard is adopted by three of the largest cloud providers.
A joint statement commits two blocs to a shared incident-notification hotline.
An export-control loophole used by several labs is closed by regulatory update.
A regional bloc agrees to fund a shared, independent model-evaluation body.
A verification protocol lets two rival labs confirm each other's safety claims without exposing model weights.
A plain-language explainer of a lab's own safety case reaches a general audience, not just specialists.
A journalist's careful piece corrects a widely repeated exaggeration about what a model can do.
A citizens' panel is convened and its questions actually shape a lab's public reporting.
A survey finds most people underestimate current capability and overestimate how well anyone understands it — and the finding gets covered.
A university course on AI risk, taught outside a lab's own funding, fills every seat.
A museum exhibit on machine learning's blind spots draws a line around the street from opening day.
A public dashboard tracking safety commitments against what's actually shipped launches, and it isn't run by a lab.
A cross-lab working group publishes a shared glossary, so at least everyone means the same thing by the same word.
A postmortem on a near-miss is published in full, names redacted, methods intact.
A retired safety researcher's memo, written for no one in particular, turns out to be exactly what a working group needed.
A student's thesis project becomes the basis for a lab's next evaluation suite.
